asDecan.p: Every sign is split into three decans of ten degrees each, and your Sun falls in the last of Scorpio's, somewhere from twenty to twenty-nine degrees. The Golden Dawn gives that slice to Venus, which is an awkward fit, to be honest. Scorpio sits opposite Taurus, one of Venus's own signs, so Venus is in detriment here and has to work against the grain. In an easy sign Venus just likes things and enjoys them. In fixed water the liking sinks in and goes private, and a good deal of it ends up playing out in your head. Mars has the first decan of Scorpio, with the Five of Cups, where a loss hits hard. The Sun has the middle one and the Six, which looks back fondly. Yours looks forward, partly because by the last ten degrees the sign is already leaning toward Sagittarius. Death is Scorpio's Major and your Sun card. The Empress is Venus's, and some of her appetite for beautiful things is in you too, kept further out of sight.

Your head runs a second life alongside the real one. You're sitting through a budget meeting and you've already moved to Lisbon, found the flat, picked the café on the corner. A new person texts and within an hour you've imagined the first holiday together, and possibly the way it ends. Friends ask what you want for your birthday and you honestly can't narrow it down, because six things would be lovely and each one comes with a whole story attached. I see this a lot with late Scorpio Suns. You're private, so most of it never gets said out loud, and people take you for calm and a bit unreadable. Meanwhile there's a whole cinema going on behind your eyes, and on a quiet evening at home you can lose two hours to a house listing in a town you've never been to.

You can see what a thing could become well before anyone else can. You walk into a tired rented flat with brown carpet, and in your head the carpet's already up, the kitchen's painted and there's a lamp in the corner where the light's bad. A friend describes a half-formed business idea over a drink, and you're the one who asks the question that makes it real, who'd actually pay for it and how much. Venus has a hard time in Scorpio, and one thing that comes out of the struggle is that the look of something never satisfies you for long. You want to know what's under it and what it might turn into. You do the same with people. You'll back the quiet colleague nobody rates, you're usually right, and they remember it for years.

Look at the figure on the card, arms half raised, staring at seven cups sitting on a cloud, a castle in one and a snake in another. You can fall for the version of something that lives in your head and then feel oddly let down by the real one. The holiday you planned for months arrives and it's fine, genuinely nice, and you spend the second day slightly flat because it isn't the one you imagined. People get the same treatment. You build someone up in private and then hold it against them when they turn out to be ordinary on a Tuesday. There's also the habit of keeping options open so you never have to find out. The course you never enrol in stays perfect, and so does the ex you never quite let go of. Venus in detriment wants a lot, and settling on one real thing can feel like losing all the others.

When life goes wrong, a job loss, a break-up, a friend who turns on you, your first move is usually to vanish into your head. You don't make a fuss. You go quiet and start planning an escape, a move interstate, a new career, a completely different life, and for a few days that fantasy does the job of keeping you upright. About a week in, the other side shows up. You might spend money you shouldn't on something that promises a fresh start, or stay up scrolling until two, or drink a bit more than usual because it softens the edges. The people close to you often feel you've left the room without going anywhere. What helps is small and dull. Pick one real thing to fix, the CV, the rent, the phone call you've been putting off, and do only that.

What people don't always spot is how much you need a partner who'll let you want things out loud. Scorpio keeps its cards close anyway, and with Venus uncomfortable in the sign, a lot of people with this decan learned young that their wishes were a bit much for the people around them, so they did their wanting in private. The partner who works is the one who asks what you'd do with a year off and listens to the whole answer, the boat, the vineyard, the pottery studio, without laughing. You also test people quietly, by watching whether they notice what you haven't said. That's a lot to ask of anyone, and a partner can fail it without ever knowing it was set. Try telling yours one daydream a week, a small one is fine, and see what they do with it.

You're usually at your best in work that runs on imagining something and then making someone want it. Design, property, marketing, fundraising, set and costume work, anything where you picture a finished thing and sell it before it exists. You're also good at reading what a client wants underneath what they ask for, which is Venus doing its job even in an awkward sign. The trouble comes around month three of any project. The exciting version in your head is done, the real version is all spreadsheets and emails, and three shinier projects have turned up in the meantime. You can end up with five things started and nothing handed in. It helps to pick one project each quarter and tell someone at work that's the one you'll finish.

At twenty this decan often lives almost entirely on possibility. You change degrees, change cities, fall hard for people who are mostly your own invention, and it can look chaotic from outside, though from the inside every change feels like the right one. By the mid-thirties most people with a late Scorpio Sun have been disappointed enough times to start testing things before falling for them. You still dream just as much, you just check the foundations first, and some of the dreams turn into an actual house, an actual business. The fifties tend to bring an ease with wanting. The Sagittarius lean in this decan shows up more, often as a taste for travel or study later in life, and you can enjoy a daydream for its own sake without feeling you have to chase it.

Keep a short list on your phone called Seven Cups. Whenever a daydream grabs you, a move, a course, a person, a big purchase, add it with the date. Once a month, read down the list and pick the one you'd be sorriest never to have tried. Within the week, take one small, real step toward it, an email, a price, a booking. Cross off anything that's lost its pull. Most months a good half of the list goes, and it's worth noticing which ones keep coming back.
